mcqs.question: Why is merge sort stable while standard quicksort and heapsort are not?
options: Merge sort is slower, and slower algorithms are always stable
Quicksort and heapsort only work on numeric data, which cannot be stable
Merge sort's merge step has an explicit tie-break that always favors the earlier-originating element, while quicksort and heapsort's comparisons have no memory of original position
Stability only applies to sorts that use extra memory
mcqs.explanation: Merge sort's stability comes from a specific implementation choice — the merge step takes from the left half on ties, and the left half always originated earlier. Quicksort's pivot-based swaps and heapsort's heap-order comparisons have no such position memory, so equal elements can end up reordered relative to each other. Neither speed nor extra memory determines stability.

mcqs.question: Which of the three classic sorts has a worst case that differs from its best case?
options: Only quicksort — merge sort and heapsort guarantee O(n log n) regardless of input shape
Only merge sort — quicksort and heapsort are both guaranteed O(n log n)
All three have identical best, average, and worst cases
Only heapsort — its heap structure can degrade on adversarial input
mcqs.explanation: Merge sort's split point is always the midpoint and heapsort's operations are governed by heap-order comparisons — neither depends on the data's shape, so both have no bad case. Quicksort's split depends on the chosen pivot and the data around it, which is exactly what opens the door to its O(n²) worst case on unlucky inputs.

mcqs.question: What does the decision-tree argument prove about comparison-based sorting algorithms?
options: Any comparison sort needs at least Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, because a binary tree distinguishing n! possible orderings needs depth at least log2(n!)
Comparison sorts can never be made stable
All comparison sorts must use O(n) extra space
Comparison sorts are always slower than non-comparison sorts like counting sort
mcqs.explanation: Modeling a comparison sort as a decision tree — each comparison a branch, each leaf a possible final ordering — requires at least n! leaves to cover every permutation, and a binary tree needs depth at least log2(n!), which is Θ(n log n). That's a floor on comparisons, unrelated to stability, memory, or a blanket claim about non-comparison sorts (which trade comparisons for structure in the keys, not speed in general).

mcqs.question: Merge sort and quicksort are both Θ(n log n), yet quicksort is usually faster in practice. Why?
options: Merge sort performs more comparisons per element than quicksort
Quicksort has a smaller theoretical complexity than merge sort
Merge sort is only faster on already-sorted input
Quicksort operates in place with contiguous, cache-friendly access and no allocation, while merge sort reads across separate regions and allocates buffers at every level
mcqs.explanation: Both are the same asymptotic class, so the real-world speed gap comes from constant factors Big-O ignores: quicksort partitions within contiguous memory with no allocation, while merge sort's merge step touches multiple regions and pays allocation and bookkeeping cost per level. Comparison counts are asymptotically similar for both, and neither statement about complexity being literally smaller or about sorted input is accurate.

mcqs.question: Heapsort has O(1) extra space and a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case, yet it's rarely the default sort in practice. Why?
options: Heapsort's worst case is actually O(n²), just like quicksort's
Heapsort cannot handle duplicate keys correctly
Its heap-index memory access pattern jumps around the array, giving poor cache locality and a larger real-world constant factor despite the identical Big-O
Heapsort requires O(n) extra space, the same as merge sort
mcqs.explanation: Heapsort's parent/child index jumps (i, 2i+1, 2i+2) scatter memory access far more than quicksort's contiguous partitioning or merge sort's sequential merge, so it tends to run slower in practice despite sharing the same asymptotic class and genuinely needing only O(1) extra space. Its worst case is O(n log n), not O(n²), and duplicates don't break it.

mcqs.question: A candidate says "merge sort, quicksort, and heapsort are all O(n log n), so it doesn't matter which one I use." What's the flaw in that reasoning?
options: It's correct — Big-O fully determines which sort to use
It ignores that only heapsort is O(n log n) in the worst case
It overlooks stability, memory footprint, and cache behavior — properties Big-O deliberately abstracts away but that determine correctness and real speed
Big-O comparisons only apply to sorts of the same data type
mcqs.explanation: Sharing an asymptotic class says nothing about stability (which can be a correctness requirement, not a nicety), memory footprint, or cache behavior, all of which differentiate these three sorts in practice. All three do share the same O(n log n) class in typical discussion of quicksort's average case, and none of this is data-type-specific.
